findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for, and what problem it solves. Within a few seconds they can say what this is and why it matters.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable."

findings.text: The page explains why an Athena page is mostly about a different project, firstmate: it is a worked example of Athena's output. Without this, a newcomer would be confused. It is still the case that most of the page is about firstmate, so someone who came to learn about Athena gets one paragraph on it and then a long technical study.
findings.source: Header: "A study is Athena's written reading of another software project, taken at one fixed commit..." and "This page is that study of firstmate."

findings.text: The next step is easy to find. A link at the top jumps to concrete install steps: git clone, ./setup.sh, prerequisites, and a sample command, `athena ask "add a changelog"`, with a note on what it does. This gives the newcomer a clear thing to do.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: Athena is described as written in Rust, but the prerequisites do not list a Rust toolchain. The page does not say whether ./setup.sh installs one, so a newcomer may not know whether they need cargo.
findings.source: Next steps: "have git 2.40 or later, a C linker, curl, and either Claude Code or npm"

findings.text: This link is aimed at the project owner, not a first-time visitor, and it sits beside the newcomer's next-step link. A newcomer may wonder whether 'your decision' means them.
findings.source: Header: "Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision."

findings.text: The firstmate study has a clear way in: a one-sentence definition, the key terms defined before they are used, and a numbered walk through one task. A newcomer can follow it without reading the dense transition cards.
findings.source: "Start here" section with "Words used first", "What firstmate is", and "One piece of work, start to finish"

findings.text: The transition cards are dense with terms specific to firstmate and repeat details from earlier sections. A newcomer is likely to skim them rather than learn from them.
findings.source: Transitions cards, e.g. t8: "A ship or scout keeps its recorded harness and needs a note; a secondmate re-reads its pin and needs none, and a secondmate with no endpoint is recovered by the spawn script instead."

findings.text: These passages use Athena's internal terms ('job', 'recorded boundary', 'studies/' folder) without explaining them, so a newcomer cannot follow them. The point that nothing was actually run does come through.
findings.source: Limits of this study, f1: "The job gave no recorded boundary for running firstmate, so no failure or retry edge was observed"; About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/"

findings.text: The claim ids link to lines in the source files at one fixed commit, which backs up the promise of traceability made in the header. A newcomer can check a statement for themselves.
findings.source: Claims and sources: each claim links to e.g. "bin/fm-spawn.sh:194-197" at the pinned commit
